Venezuela’s Fisheries Sector Faces Severe Debt Crisis as Export Revenue Plummets

Venezuela’s fisheries industry is reeling from a rapidly escalating debt crisis, with mounting loan defaults and a freeze in access to working capital threatening to halt operations across major processing hubs. Industry sources report that the sharp fall in export prices for key products such as shrimp and tuna, combined with a sudden drop in overseas demand, has left fishing firms unable to meet their debt obligations or pay workers on time.

According to the Venezuelan Fisheries Confederation, over 60% of medium and large fishing companies in the eastern coastal region have entered technical default since April. “The situation is unprecedented,” said Rafael Herrera, president of the confederation. “Many firms are now months behind on repayments, and the sector’s access to credit lines has evaporated.”

Sources at Puerto Azul Fishing Cooperative, one of the country’s largest operators, say their main processing plant in Sucre state has reduced output by 70% and furloughed over half its workforce. “We can’t afford fuel or repairs for our vessels, and many boats are docked indefinitely,” a company manager said.

The National Union of Fisheries Workers estimates that more than 9,000 jobs have been directly affected in the past six weeks, with hundreds of contract workers reporting unpaid wages. “Families are struggling to cope as the season’s earnings disappear,” said union leader Alicia Romero.

Analysts warn that, without a rebound in export demand or emergency financial support, the crisis could force widespread shutdowns of landing sites and processing facilities. As of this week, industry leaders are appealing for government intervention to stabilize the sector and prevent further job losses.
